Today, he is here to share his insights into the double strategy, and we welcome all those coaches from across Australia and across the world. Louis, if we'd like to get started. In your sessions, you like to cover offence, defence and neutral situations. On the court, what does that look like? Okay, so first of all, the reason why I want to cover offence and control defence, because it happens all the time. And the challenge is to develop skills and maintain them. So if I do that all the time, I gradually improve these skills, and they are always maintained by the fact that I always train on them. So some of my colleagues sometime will train for one month offence, and after that the one month defence and just the maintenance is not sustainable enough. So how does that start? Let's say because we're doubles, they're rallying cross court. After they rally cross court, one guy hits the ball quite easy, and the other guy really attacks it as hard as he can. And he has to make up the five attacking shots in a row, and the guy will receive it because it's double.

It's he will look to either make a real good defensive shot, like a lob back, but a real nice lob, or he will look to neutralise back, like keeping the ball in a way that it's hard to attack again, or he will look to counter attack, which means either hit the ball hard back or place the ball very accurately back. So by training to attack and to defend, each time they practice their cross court, it's very important. Then they go to the net, and this is volley against ground strokes. After they have a good tempo, they feel like comfortable with the warm-up. They throw an easy ball, and they ask their friend to hit hazard as they can on them. So, and then they have to practice their defensive volleys. And same thing. The first thing is don't miss your volley. Second, neutralise by balling back to the back end of the two guys. Don't give, we have a rule to not give two forehands in a row. So they have to volley toward the back end to neutralise. And the third option is look to even put the ball away if you can try to make a good angle of stuff like this. But when the guy is very hard, we look more to neutralise. Not missing is always good. If you can't control the ball, then your defensive volleys is better. Trying to make a winner on that will be a bit too risky and it will lead to too many errors. And same thing after that.
